overview: In late-sixteenth- and early-seventeenth-century Genoa, mercantile wealth reshaped streets, houses and hospitality. The Rolli palaces reveal how private residences served the republic's public business.

items.text: In the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, Genoa developed the Strade Nuove as a coordinated district of streets and aristocratic palaces above the older city.
The palaces adapted to steep and confined sites with open staircases, courtyards and garden-facing loggias. Frescoes and stucco decorated their interiors.
The Senate established the Rolli list of private palaces used to lodge distinguished official visitors. Hosting state guests became an obligation attached to selected elite homes.
The Rolli system sorted residences into categories corresponding to different ranks of guest. Hospitality made social hierarchy part of the organization of official visits.
Architectural treatises spread knowledge of Genoa's new streets and palaces beyond the city in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

sources.title: UNESCO, Genoa: Le Strade Nuove and the Palazzi dei Rolli
